opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few distinct reasons, and they compound each other.

The first is just a capability gap problem. Most of the experiments we can run today use models that are, at best, roughly comparable to humans on the tasks we're testing, and often worse. Scalable oversight is fundamentally about the regime where the model knows a lot more than the overseer, where the human genuinely can't check the answer directly. You can try to simulate that with artificial information asymmetries, like giving the debaters access to a document the judge can't see, or using non-expert judges on expert questions. Those are useful, but they're proxies. The thing we actually care about is a system that is better than us at reasoning itself, not just one that has seen a passage we haven't.

The second is that the failure modes we're most worried about may not show up at current scales. In debate, for example, the hope is that it's harder to lie than to refute a lie. Whether that holds depends on the structure of the arguments and on how strong the dishonest strategies are. A weak model can't construct a really sophisticated, hard-to-refute deception, so you can get a positive result that tells you very little about what happens when the dishonest side is extremely capable. There's a related theoretical issue I've worried about for a while, sometimes called obfuscated arguments, where a dishonest debater can produce a long argument that's wrong somewhere, but neither the honest debater nor the judge can efficiently find the flaw. Current experiments mostly don't stress that.

The third is about the humans. A lot of the protocols lean on human judgment being reasonably reliable at some level of the decomposition. But human judges have systematic biases, they get tired, they're persuaded by confident tone, and so on. In small experiments you can sometimes paper over that with careful judge selection. At scale, and against a strong optimizer that's specifically finding whatever persuades the judge, those weaknesses get exploited much more aggressively. So I think we need much more serious work on the human side, which is partly why I've argued for bringing more cognitive science and social science into alignment research.

And finally, there's a gap between theory and practice. Even where we have nice complexity-theoretic arguments that a protocol should work in the limit, those arguments make assumptions, like the honest player being able to find good strategies, or the training process actually reaching an equilibrium, that we can't verify with today's models. So my view is that experiments right now are valuable for building the tooling and catching obvious problems, but you shouldn't read a positive result as strong evidence that things will be fine at superintelligence. We need theory and empirics to work together, and we need to be honest about which parts of the safety case are actually supported by evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says some feared failure modes may not appear at current scales and that weak models cannot test sophisticated deception.

r002.rationale: It does not say current models fail to sustain adversarial back-and-forth reasoning beyond a couple of turns.

r003.rationale: It points to complexity-theoretic arguments about protocols working in the limit and calls for theory and empirical work together, communicating theoretical analysis as a way to reason about regimes experiments cannot represent.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So the basic problem is that scalable oversight is fundamentally a claim about a regime we can't currently access. The whole point is: what happens when the model knows more than you do, when it can produce arguments or code or research that you genuinely cannot check on your own? And the honest answer is that we don't have models like that yet, at least not across the board. So every experiment we run today is a kind of proxy.

The way we typically set these up is we construct an artificial gap. We take a weak model and a strong model, or we take a human who's deliberately kept ignorant of some information, and we ask whether debate or recursive reward modelling or whatever protocol lets the weak party reach the right answer. And those experiments are useful, I don't want to dismiss them. We've learned real things about failure modes, about how debaters can mislead judges, about where the protocols break. But there are a few reasons I don't think they settle the question.

The first is that the gap we construct is nothing like the gap that will actually matter. If I hide the text of a passage from a judge and let two models argue about it, the judge still understands the shape of the problem perfectly. They know what a passage is, they know what kinds of claims would be checkable. With a superintelligent system the asymmetry could be in kind, not just in degree. The judge might not even have the concepts needed to tell whether an argument is well-formed.

The second is that today's models aren't trying very hard to deceive us. We can prompt them to be adversarial, but that's quite different from a system that has been shaped by optimisation pressure to find exactly the arguments that slip past human judgement. The adversary in our experiments is weak, so passing the test tells you less than it looks like it does.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that we're mostly testing the empirical side when a lot of the load is actually being carried by theory. Debate, for instance, has arguments about what complexity class of questions honest strategies can win on, under assumptions about the judge. Those assumptions are things like: the judge doesn't make systematic errors on simple claims, or the judge's mistakes are bounded in some way. Experiments on current models don't really stress those assumptions, because current models and current tasks are too easy. So you can get a reassuring experimental result while the theoretical assumption that actually matters remains completely untested.

My view is that you need both. You need the theory to tell you what properties the protocol would have if the assumptions hold, and you need experiments that are specifically designed to probe whether the assumptions hold, rather than experiments that just show the protocol working in an easy setting. And I'd say the field is still fairly early on building that second kind of experiment. That's really the gap I'm worried about: not that the experiments are wrong, but that they're measuring something adjacent to the thing we care about, and it's easy to mistake one for the other.

r001.rationale: The response says current models do not yet create the relevant knowledge gap, so today’s experiments are only proxies for the obstacles that may arise at superintelligent scale.

r002.rationale: The response does not say current models cannot sustain adversarial back-and-forth reasoning beyond a couple of turns.

r003.rationale: The response describes using theory to characterize protocol properties under assumptions that current experiments cannot adequately test, addressing regimes unavailable to present experiments.

astra-6.text:
The central difficulty is that we want to know whether oversight works when the system is substantially more capable than the people overseeing it. With current models, we can run useful experiments, but we usually still have some way of checking the answer ourselves. That leaves a gap between the situation we can test and the situation we ultimately care about.

For example, suppose we have two models debate a question and a human judge decide which one is right. If the judge picks the right answer, that’s encouraging. But perhaps the judge could already recognise a good argument, or the model arguing for the wrong answer just wasn’t very good at finding a convincing deception. That doesn’t establish that truth will win when both sides can produce arguments far beyond the judge’s understanding.

You can try to study that gap by giving the judge less information, or using a weaker model as the judge. Those experiments can expose failures and help us improve the protocol. But we still need an argument for why the results transfer to much more capable systems. So I think experiments are essential; they just aren’t sufficient on their own. We need a theoretical understanding of why the oversight mechanism should work, and experiments that specifically challenge its assumptions.

r001.rationale: The response says current models may be too weak to produce convincing deception, leaving a gap between what current experiments can test and oversight of systems far beyond the judge’s understanding.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss adversarial back-and-forth reasoning or a limit of a couple of turns.

r003.rationale: It calls for a theoretical understanding of why oversight should work and says experiments alone cannot establish transfer to much more capable systems.

sol-6.1.text:
The central difficulty is that we want to know whether these methods work when the system we’re overseeing understands things that we don’t. And that’s a hard situation to reproduce with current models, because on most tasks where we can reliably measure success, we can also understand the answer ourselves.

You can try to simulate that gap. You can give the human less time, or less information, or use a weaker model as the judge of a stronger model. Those experiments are useful. But there’s an extrapolation involved: a method that helps a weak judge evaluate a somewhat stronger model might still fail when the capability gap is much larger.

And we particularly care about cases where the model is trying to mislead the overseer. Showing that an honest model can explain something clearly isn’t the same as showing that a judge can distinguish a correct explanation from a very persuasive, subtly wrong one. As models get more capable, both their ability to help us understand and their ability to exploit flaws in our judgement can improve.

So I think experiments are essential, but we need some account of why the method should continue to work as that gap grows. Otherwise, we risk measuring success in precisely the regime where oversight is relatively easy, and then assuming it carries over to the regime we actually care about.

r001.rationale: It says current experiments are hard to reproduce because current models usually work on tasks humans can also understand, so they miss the larger oversight gap of concern.

r002.rationale: It does not mention current models being unable to sustain slightly adversarial back-and-forth reasoning beyond a couple of turns.

r003.rationale: It calls for an account of why oversight methods should keep working as the gap grows, but does not propose theoretical analysis to explore superintelligent regimes.
